The juxtaposition is instructive: while Anthropic's Claude Code has captured imaginations with demonstrations of end-to-end software development, Nous Research is betting that open-source alternatives trained on verifiable problems can close the gap — and that transparency in how these models are built matters as much as raw capability. What distinguishes the NousCoder-14B release from many competitor announcements is its radical openness. Nous Research published not just the model weights but the complete reinforcement learning environment, benchmark suite, and training harness — built on the company's Atropos framework — enabling any researcher with sufficient compute to reproduce or extend the work. "Open-sourcing the Atropos stack provides the necessary infrastructure for reproducible olympiad-level reasoning research," noted one observer on X, summarizing the significance for the academic and open-source communities. The model was trained by Joe Li, a researcher in residence at Nous Research and a former competitive programmer himself. Li's technical report reveals an unexpectedly personal dimension: he compared the model's improvement trajectory to his own journey on Codeforces, the competitive programming platform where participants earn ratings based on contest performance. Based on rough estimates mapping LiveCodeBench scores to Codeforces ratings, Li calculated that NousCoder-14B's improvemen t— from approximately the 1600-1750 rating range to 2100-2200 — mirrors a leap that took him nearly two years of sustained practice between ages 14 and 16. The model accomplished the equivalent in four days. "Watching that final training run unfold was quite a surreal experience," Li wrote in the technical report. But Li was quick to note an important caveat that speaks to broader questions about AI efficiency: he solved roughly 1,000 problems during those two years, while the model required 24,000. Humans, at least for now, remain dramatically more sample-efficient learners. NousCoder-14B's training process offers a window into the increasingly sophisticated techniques researchers use to improve AI reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning. The approach relies on what researchers call "verifiable rewards" — a system where the model generates code solutions, those solutions are executed against test cases, and the model receives a simple binary signal: correct or incorrect. This feedback loop, while conceptually straightforward, requires significant infrastructure to execute at scale. Nous Research used Modal, a cloud computing platform, to run sandboxed code execution in parallel. Each of the 24,000 training problems contains hundreds of test cases on average, and the system must verify that generated code produces correct outputs within time and memory constraints — 15 seconds and 4 gigabytes, respectively. The training employed a technique called DAPO (Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization), which the researchers found performed slightly better than alternatives in their experiments. A key innovation involves "dynamic sampling" — discarding training examples where the model either solves all attempts or fails all attempts, since these provide no useful gradient signal for learning. The researchers also adopted "iterative context extension," first training the model with a 32,000-token context window before expanding to 40,000 tokens. During evaluation, extending the context further to approximately 80,000 tokens produced the best results, with accuracy reaching 67.87 percent. Perhaps most significantly, the training pipeline overlaps inference and verification — as soon as the model generates a solution, it begins work on the next problem while the previous solution is being checked. This pipelining, combined with asynchronous training where multiple model instances work in parallel, maximizes hardware utilization on expensive GPU clusters. Buried in Li's technical report is a finding with significant implications for the future of AI development: the training dataset for NousCoder-14B encompasses "a significant portion of all readily available, verifiable competitive programming problems in a standardized dataset format." In other words, for this particular domain, the researchers are approaching the limits of high-quality training data. "The total number of competitive programming problems on the Internet is roughly the same order of magnitude," Li wrote, referring to the 24,000 problems used for training. "This suggests that within the competitive programming domain, we have approached the limits of high-quality data." This observation echoes growing concern across the AI industry about data constraints. While compute continues to scale according to well-understood economic and engineering principles, training data is "increasingly finite," as Li put it. "It appears that some of the most important research that needs to be done in the future will be in the areas of synthetic data generation and data efficient algorithms and architectures," he concluded. The challenge is particularly acute for competitive programming because the domain requires problems with known correct solutions that can be verified automatically. Unlike natural language tasks where human evaluation or proxy metrics suffice, code either works or it doesn't — making synthetic data generation considerably more difficult. Li identified one potential avenue: training models not just to solve problems but to generate solvable problems, enabling a form of self-play similar to techniques that proved successful in game-playing AI systems. "Once synthetic problem generation is solved, self-play becomes a very interesting direction," he wrote. Nous Research has carved out a distinctive position in the AI landscape: a company committed to open-source releases that compete with — and sometimes exceed — proprietary alternatives. The company raised $50 million in April 2025 in a round led by Paradigm, the cryptocurrency-focused venture firm founded by Coinbase co-founder Fred Ehrsam. Total funding reached $65 million, according to some reports. The investment reflected growing interest in decentralized approaches to AI training, an area where Nous Research has developed its Psyche platform. Previous releases include Hermes 4, a family of models that we reported "outperform ChatGPT without content restrictions," and DeepHermes-3, which the company described as the first "toggle-on reasoning model" — allowing users to activate extended thinking capabilities on demand. The company has cultivated a distinctive aesthetic and community, prompting some skepticism about whether style might overshadow substance. "Ofc i'm gonna believe an anime pfp company. stop benchmarkmaxxing ffs," wrote one critic on X, referring to Nous Research's anime-style branding and the industry practice of optimizing for benchmark performance. Others raised technical questions. "Based on the benchmark, Nemotron is better," noted one commenter, referring to Nvidia's family of language models. Another asked whether NousCoder-14B is "agentic focused or just 'one shot' coding" — a distinction that matters for practical software development, where iterating on feedback typically produces better results than single attempts. The release includes several directions for future work that hint at where AI coding research may be heading. Multi-turn reinforcement learning tops the list. Currently, the model receives only a final binary reward — pass or fail — after generating a solution. But competitive programming problems typically include public test cases that provide intermediate feedback: compilation errors, incorrect outputs, time limit violations. Training models to incorporate this feedback across multiple attempts could significantly improve performance. Controlling response length also remains a challenge. The researchers found that incorrect solutions tended to be longer than correct ones, and response lengths quickly saturated available context windows during training — a pattern that various algorithmic modifications failed to resolve. Perhaps most ambitiously, Li proposed "problem generation and self-play" — training models to both solve and create programming problems. This would address the data scarcity problem directly by enabling models to generate their own training curricula. "Humans are great at generating interesting and useful problems for other competitive programmers, but it appears that there still exists a significant gap in LLM capabilities in creative problem generation," Li wrote. The model is available now on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. For researchers and developers who want to build on the work, Nous Research has published the complete Atropos training stack alongside it. What took Li two years of adolescent dedication to achieve—climbing from a 1600-level novice to a 2100-rated competitor on Codeforces—an AI replicated in 96 hours. He needed 1,000 problems. The model needed 24,000. But soon enough, these systems may learn to write their own problems, teach themselves, and leave human benchmarks behind entirely. The question is no longer whether machines can learn to code. It's whether they'll soon be better teachers than we ever were.

articles.headline: OpenAI previews Ultrafast API tier for GPT-5.6 Sol
articles.blurb: OpenAI's UltraOpenAI's Ultrafast API service tier can run GPT-5.6 Sol at 750 output tokens per second, 14 times the speed of Standard. The service is designed for products and workflows in which delays can determine whether an answer remains useful. Access is initially restricted to a select group of customers. Powered by Cerebras, a wider rollout is planned as capacity grows.

articles.headline: X open sources its ranking algorithm, letting users see if they've been ‘shadowbanned'
articles.blurb: X has open-sourced its 'For You' algorithm and its core ranking engine under the Apache v2 license. The company has also expanded its previous efforts to open source parts of its codebase to add more detail, making it roughly 10 to 15 times larger than it was before. X is providing tools that will let users see for themselves if and how its ranking systems have impacted their account or posts. The tool will be available to a test group of accounts for at least a year as a pilot before rolling out more broadly.

articles.headline: Driver Sets Record for Hydrogen-Powered Vehicle at More Than 406 MPH
articles.blurb: Andy Green set a record for the fastest land speed driving a JCB Hydromax on Tuesday at 406.320 miles per hour. The hydrogen-fueled internal-combustion vehicle took about 72 seconds to get from 50 miles per hour to 400. At 64, Green is the only person to break the sound barrier on land, driving a jet-powered car at an average speed of 763.035 miles per hour in 1997. The JCB Hydromax was not built to rival that record, but to set a new fastest speed for a hydrogen vehicle - the previous record for a hydrogen combustion vehicle was 185.5 miles per hour, set in 2004 by the BMW H2R.

articles.headline: America Wants to Make Its Own Humanoid Robots. That Won't Be Easy
articles.blurb: China has a near-total dominance of the supply chain, so building a robot entirely free of Chinese parts is not practical. The Chinese robotics industry was built on billions of dollars in state funding. Fledgling robot makers in the US will need substantial financial and policy support to compete. The US humanoid robotics industry is still in its infancy, and makers of non-humanoid robots are struggling to compete with Chinese rivals.

articles.headline: DeepSeek Harness (Website)
articles.blurb: DeepSeek Harness is now in developer preview, with source code included. Every capability is a plugin that can be swapped or recomposed. Developers can select, swap, or extend any capability in the configuration without changing the DeepSeek Harness source code. Everything the model sees is recorded in an append-only session log.

articles.headline: Foreman (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Foreman is an eve software factory that puts AI agents on every stage of the development loop and keeps people on the judgment calls. It takes tasks from GitHub and Linear, moves each one through four stations - Classifier, Analyst, Implementer, and Reviewer - and delivers a reviewed draft pull request on the repository. The Classifier triages the task, the Analyst turns it into a plan with acceptance criteria, the Implementer executes the plan in its own sandbox, and the Reviewer independently judges everything against the real diff. Developers just review, mark ready, and merge.

articles.headline: Pangram, Authorship, and French Theory
articles.blurb: Being called out for using AI is the new way of dunking on people and posts. However, this calling out is a social function that isn't just 'AI bad'. People want authorship because it has meaning. Several AI labs have recently made announcements about watermarking outputs for easy AI detection.

articles.headline: The DeepSeek Thesis
articles.blurb: Liang Wenfeng, CEO of DeepSeek, is now richer than both Dario Amodei and Sam Altman. His little-known group of researchers has managed to consistently command the world's attention. Backed by the immense wealth of his hedge fund, they keep giving their work away for free. Liang believes that there is an inevitable causal relationship between automated learning and generalized intelligence, and that the pursuit of such advanced machine intelligence is the only problem worth solving right now.

articles.headline: Musk Hints Starlink Is Coming to Future Teslas as Cybercab Shows Integrated Dish
articles.blurb: Elon Musk says that Starlink will eventually be necessary to provide the amount of bandwidth connected vehicles will require.

articles.blurb: An overview of Foreman's runtime map that covers what runs where, how the filesystem defines the agent, and the three boundaries that shape the design.

articles.headline: OpenAI's Revenue Run Rate Tops $40 Billion Ahead of IPO
articles.blurb: OpenAI has roughly doubled its run rate from the end of 2025 due to the growth of its AI coding software, momentum from subscription sales and its nascent advertising business, and its core consumer business.

articles.blurb: Navigating codebases as a human is becoming an exercise in futility as more and more explanatory artifacts are being generated rather than written.

articles.headline: Introducing Bluesky Protocol Services
articles.blurb: Bluesky Protocol Services organizes all the documentation developers need within the ecosystem, clarifies the service contracts around Bluesky-provided infrastructure, replaces the old docs site, and gives the team a clean way to ship future releases.

articles.headline: Even Claude Is in the Dark About Dario Amodei's Wife—and Her Influence at Anthropic
articles.blurb: Cami Clark keeps a low profile, but is a key adviser to Anthropic chief Dario Amodei.

articles.headline: Compute Scarcity Is Permanent. Build a Ladder
articles.blurb: Processors are currently scarce because of the same bottleneck: the high-bandwidth memory and the advanced packaging that binds it to the die are capacity-limited across the entire industry. This can't be fixed with a bigger cloud budget or a patient retry loop. This constraint isn't clearing anytime soon and is likely a permanent condition. Businesses need to build for this reality rather than waiting for the shortage to end.

articles.headline: The rise of the 1-person growth engineer
articles.blurb: No industry leader has created a program or certification for AI fluency yet. It's difficult for individuals and hiring managers to understand whether they're doing cutting-edge work or are part of the status quo. Building a portfolio of proof is really important at this stage. Do the work in public, talk about what you're building, and collect third-party proof and outcomes wherever you can get them.

articles.headline: 99% of My Website Traffic Is Bots
articles.blurb: PatronView is a donor-research database with 1.5 million profile pages built from public records. In one week, its server served 1.28 million pages while analytics counted only 5,977 pageviews. That is 214 invisible loads for every visible one. Claude-SearchBot crawled 35,000 pages for every visitor it sent back. Amazon crawled 117,000 pages a day and sent none. Cloudflare's bot detector added 2.875 seconds and cut mobile Lighthouse to 58. Removing it restored 99, then an Azure scraper pulled 23,000 pages in an hour. The founder now judges crawlers by pages taken per visitor returned.

articles.headline: Inside an Applied AI company
articles.blurb: Applied AI companies sell completed work, making the harness, not the model, the core product: tools, integrations, persistence, orchestration, oversight, and evals close the gap from 70% to 98%+ accuracy. Durable advantage comes from compounding knowledge, hardening, and evaluation loops.

articles.headline: How to keep thinking
articles.blurb: One engineer now runs six or seven AI-agent sessions on the same coding task. Some explore, others build competing versions, and more review and test. Things got faster, but his job slowly became skimming and judging answers instead of forming his own. So he added one deliberately slow habit. He reads dense nonfiction and writes about it without an LLM. As more research, code, and analysis move into agent queues, keep one place where you still have to start with a blank page and decide what you think.

articles.headline: Google Launches Gemini 3.7 Flash With a 50% Price Cut Through December
articles.blurb: Google has released Gemini 3.7 Flash, three weeks after Gemini 3.6 Flash. Until December 31, API rates are $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. The rates double on January 1. The offer gives developers a defined testing window.

articles.headline: ChatGPT Ads Get Automated Bidding, Placements, and URL Parameters
articles.blurb: OpenAI has added three new features to its ads platform. The platform will now automatically adjust bids to get the most results from advertisers' budgets. A new Eligible Platforms dropdown allows advertisers to individually deselect ad platforms. There are now new ways to include URL parameters for third-party tracking.

articles.headline: ChatGPT for Mac adds opt-in Computer History feature, replacing Chronicle
articles.blurb: ChatGPT's new Computer History feature creates a searchable timeline from activity across selected apps and websites. The feature is off by default and must be enabled by each user. Computer History replaces the Chronicle research preview. While Chronicle relied on screenshots, Computer History records interaction events exposed through macOS accessibility features.

articles.headline: Land a ‘Buffalo' to Establish a New Market
articles.blurb: A sales consultant advised a portfolio company with a greenfield market to focus on one vertical and target large enterprises. The strategy involves attending conferences, creating vertical-specific content, and landing key industry leaders as references. Once established, the company should expand into related verticals to leverage their initial success.

articles.headline: The moat paradox
articles.blurb: Building a business moat involves solving the hardest core problems, not just relying on Helmer's seven lagging indicators. The leading indicator for a defensible business is solving high-effort, high-risk problems directly tied to core user value. Fear of uncertainty often deters entrepreneurs, but confronting difficult problems can create a sustainable competitive advantage.

articles.headline: The Car Got Better. The Deal Got Worse.
articles.blurb: US automakers made cars safer and longer-lived, while like-for-like prices fell roughly 45% after inflation.

articles.headline: Analyzing the evidence that helps businesses win “product not received” disputes
articles.blurb: Stripe studied one million "product not received" disputes to learn what evidence actually wins.

articles.headline: TikTok Shop is increasingly attracting brands selling high-ticket items
articles.blurb: Mellow Sleep sells pillows and comforters on TikTok Shop, where bulky products once looked like a bad fit.

articles.headline: Announcing: Docker VMM Public Beta
articles.blurb: Docker has released a public beta of Docker VMM, a new first-party virtualization layer built in-house, available in Docker Desktop v4.86 for Mac and Windows. The new engine replaces the third-party VMM Docker Desktop previously relied on, and promises faster container startup, better file I/O, and smarter memory management that returns RAM to the host when containers are idle. Windows users can opt in via Settings, General, and the Docker VMM option. General availability is targeted for the end of October, when Docker VMM becomes the default engine for new installs across Mac, Windows, and Linux.

articles.headline: Smart Routing in Unity AI Gateway: Match frontier quality with 30%+ lower cost per task
articles.blurb: Databricks has launched Smart Routing in Beta through its Unity AI Gateway, a system that automatically matches coding tasks to models based on complexity rather than defaulting to the most expensive option. On internal workloads, Smart Routing outperformed any single model at 65% of the cost per task compared to a leading model like Opus 5, and matched Opus 5 on public benchmarks at less than half the cost. The system works natively inside Claude Code and Codex, and also runs through Omnigent, Databricks' meta-harness that routes across both models and coding harnesses. A lightweight classifier reads each task and labels it across several fields before the router decides whether to escalate to a frontier model or delegate to a cheaper one.

articles.headline: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering
articles.blurb: AI has made code generation dramatically faster without making review, debugging, or architectural understanding equally cheap, allowing bad decisions and technical debt to accumulate much faster than before. Engineers who can evaluate tradeoffs, understand complex systems, and take responsibility for AI-generated changes may become more valuable, while implementation skill alone becomes less differentiating.

articles.headline: Octopus Easy Mode - Progressive Rollout
articles.blurb: Octopus Easy Mode demonstrates progressive rollouts by promoting the same release through Development, Prod 10, Prod 50, and Prod 100 environments, with validation gates stopping failed deployments. A runbook uses delayed API calls to automatically advance successful deployments, while environments provide clearer lifecycle visualization and release progression controls than tenants.

articles.headline: How to Choose Digital Experience Monitoring Tools
articles.blurb: Digital experience monitoring measures user-facing performance through RUM, synthetic monitoring, session replay, and endpoint monitoring, complementing APM by connecting frontend issues with backend telemetry. The guide emphasizes unified observability, privacy controls, integration, and total cost when evaluating DEM platforms such as New Relic, Datadog, Dynatrace, ThousandEyes, and Catchpoint.

articles.headline: Spiderfoot (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: SpiderFoot is an open source, OSINT automation tool written in Python 3 that integrates with over 200 data source modules. It can be run via a web-based interface or the command line. The tool supports both offensive and defensive use cases, including penetration testing and monitoring an organization's internet exposure.

articles.headline: Switchyard (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Switchyard is an open-source Rust proxy and library for routing LLM traffic across providers, released under the Apache 2.0 license by NVIDIA Corporation. It translates between OpenAI Chat, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages formats, so coding agents like Claude Code or Codex can talk to backends like vLLM, Ollama, or NVIDIA NIM without changing their native API calls. The project is pre-alpha and not intended for production use, with the API expected to change significantly before v1.0.

articles.headline: Beszel (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Beszel is a lightweight server monitoring platform that includes Docker statistics, historical data, and alert functions. It has a friendly web interface, simple configuration, and is ready to use out of the box. Beszel supports automatic backup, multi-user, OAuth authentication, and API access.

articles.headline: Cloudflare Launches Persistent, Stateful, Computer-like Environments for Agents
articles.blurb: Cloudflare Computer is an open-source runtime for AI agents that combines scalable Cloudflare isolates with on-demand containers and browsers, reducing reliance on costly ephemeral containers. Its shared SQLite-based filesystem lets agents move between execution environments while preserving state, with auditing and observability built in, though the system remains an early preview.

articles.headline: How we tracked down a 16-year-old SQLite bug
articles.blurb: A rare race condition between SQLite WAL checkpointing and concurrent writes could permanently lose committed pages and corrupt databases, a bug that had existed for at least 16 years. Tailscale uncovered it after months of production forensics and 19 corruption incidents, working with SQLite maintainers to build new VFS tracing that isolated the race and led to a fix released in SQLite 3.51.3.

articles.headline: Good apps aren't born, they're guided: Building observable policy as code
articles.blurb: VictoriaMetrics and Kyverno have published a guide on combining Kubernetes-native policy enforcement with time-series observability using open-source tooling.

articles.headline: Keeping ChatGPT Fast as AI Development Accelerates
articles.blurb: Agentic development has sharply increased code change volume and parallelism at OpenAI, creating hidden performance, resource, and scalability costs beyond GPUs.

articles.headline: Adyen expands Toast partnership into the US
articles.blurb: Adyen is expanding its partnership with Toast into the US, adding its payments infrastructure to a platform that facilitated more than $215 billion in GPV across roughly 180,000 locations over the past year. The deal extends a relationship already spanning Ireland, the UK, Canada, and Australia, while giving Toast greater processing stability and creating potential to embed more Adyen financial products into its restaurant and retail platform.

articles.headline: Cloudflare launches Cloudflare Wallets
articles.blurb: Cloudflare Wallets is a programmable wallet for the agentic Internet. Starting today, you can claim a Cloudflare Wallet handle for your account, which will provide a unique username to help you better connect with merchants. Soon, you will be able to set up and use your Cloudflare Wallet to pay for APIs and content.

articles.headline: Monzo tops one million business accounts
articles.blurb: Monzo has become the first British digital bank to surpass one million business customers. Having launched the service in 2020, the online-only bank has seen numbers double in just the past two years, posing a challenge to the dominance of the UK's Big Four banks: Barclays, HSBC, NatWest, and Lloyds.

articles.headline: The FDIC wants a rulebook for bank-fintech partnerships
articles.blurb: The FDIC is working with major banking and fintech trade groups on a voluntary standard-setting and certification body for bank-fintech partnerships, signaling a shift toward clearer baseline controls after years of BaaS failures and regulatory fallout. The post also covers Block moving more payments onto its own bank rails, Chime's second consecutive GAAP-profitable quarter, Polymarket's potential $20B+ valuation, Bunq's rejected US charter application, and Cloudflare's push into AI-agent wallets and payments.

articles.headline: Why investors are backing AI-native fintech startups built for speed
articles.blurb: Investors are increasingly favoring AI-native fintech startups that can ship faster, scale with leaner teams, and generate more revenue per employee, even as broader fintech deal activity declines. Durable winners will pair that speed with proprietary data infrastructure, disciplined AI deployment, and strong accuracy and security controls rather than simply layering AI onto existing workflows.

articles.headline: TransUnion warns lenders on private student loan risk after US rules
articles.blurb: New federal borrowing caps could push more student borrowers toward private financing, but TransUnion says lenders will need to be selective about who they serve. Roughly 30% of federal borrowers in repayment are at least 90 days delinquent, compared with about 3% for unsecured personal loans, creating significant underwriting risk as private lenders pursue new originations and refinancing opportunities.

articles.headline: Robinhood brings zero-fee digital asset trading to UK
articles.blurb: Robinhood is adding more than 50 digital assets to its UK investment app through Bitstamp, with no trading, account maintenance, or custody fees. The rollout also includes Cortex Digests, a generative AI tool that explains market moves in plain English, as Robinhood pushes to become an all-in-one investing platform spanning stocks, options, futures, and crypto.

articles.headline: Klarna goes live with JP Morgan Payments for US merchants
articles.blurb: Klarna is now integrated into JP Morgan Payments' Commerce Platform, allowing US merchants to offer pay-in-full, interest-free installment, and longer-term financing options without a separate integration. The partnership gives Klarna distribution through the largest US merchant acquirer, which processes $2.6 trillion annually, while helping JP Morgan merchants add flexible checkout options with less implementation work.

articles.headline: Uber invests in Chile fintech in push into motorbike loans
articles.blurb: Uber is backing Chilean fintech Galgo, which has deployed more than $400 million in credit and will develop lower-cost motorcycle financing exclusively for Uber delivery workers. Galgo, now profitable and generating roughly $100 million in annualized revenue, plans to enter another Latin American market next year and use the partnership to invest further in technology, data, and AI. The deal extends Uber's push into vehicle financing after its 2024 investment in mobility fintech Moove.

articles.headline: Repeat founder Ryan Williams raises $10M seed for an AI startup for private credit managers
articles.blurb: Ellis AI is building AI agents to automate the fragmented back-office work of private credit firms, connecting existing documents, accounting systems, and spreadsheets in one platform. The agents can monitor portfolios, flag data discrepancies, prepare reports, and help close monthly books, while leaving material decisions to human managers. Founder Ryan Williams previously co-founded real estate investment platform Cadre, which raised more than $160 million before being acquired by Yieldstreet in 2024.

articles.headline: US regulator rejects Bunq's banking license application
articles.blurb: The OCC rejected Dutch fintech Bunq's application for a US banking license, citing concerns over whether the company would maintain sufficient capital and whether management had enough experience with unsecured credit cards.

articles.headline: Google Pay introduces Gemini-enabled AI tool for users in India
articles.blurb: Google Pay is turning its payments app into more of a personal finance assistant, letting Indian users ask Gemini questions about their spending, get categorized breakdowns, identify savings opportunities, and learn about topics like credit scores and investing.

articles.headline: Who’s Tracking You? Use This New Service to Find Out
articles.blurb: It can be daunting to determine who's responsible for showing ads on the websites we visit, or who's harvesting data from the mobile apps we use every day. That information is already semi-public, but it is not easily parsed and traditionally much of it has remained walled away in the hands of large advertising platforms. Not anymore: A powerful and free new service called DecryptAds scrapes and correlates this adtech data and makes it simple to quickly learn a great deal about the entities that are tracking you.

articles.headline: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 400 Security Holes
articles.blurb: Microsoft today released updates to remedy at least 398 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software, including one weakness that is already being actively exploited and two others that were publicly detailed prior to today.

articles.headline: Canadian Man Pleads Guilty in Snowflake Extortions
articles.blurb: A 26-year-old Canadian man once described as one of the most consequential cybercrime threat actors of 2024 has pleaded guilty to computer fraud and conspiracy to hack and extort more than 165 organizations that used the cloud data storage provider Snowflake. Connor Riley Moucka, of Kitchener, Ontario, also admitted to stealing call and text history records of more than 100 million AT&T customers.

articles.headline: Read This Before You Buy That TV Streaming Stick
articles.blurb: Security experts have been sounding the alarm for years about the risks of using generic TV boxes that promise unlimited content streaming for a one-time fee, warning that they secretly rent the user's Internet connection out to strangers. But a groundbreaking new analysis finds these devices also routinely spoof themselves as mobile phones clicking ads on AI-generated websites as part of sprawling operation that seeks to defraud online merchants and advertising networks.

articles.headline: LG to Ban Residential Proxies from Smart TV Apps
articles.blurb: The home appliance giant LG Electronics USA said this week it plans to suspend any apps built for its smart TVs that turn one's television into an always-on residential proxy node. The move comes less than a month after researchers found that more than 42 percent of games and other apps available for download on LG's webOS store allow unknown third-parties to route their Internet traffic through a user's TV.

articles.headline: Microsoft Patches a Record 570 Security Flaws
articles.blurb: Microsoft Corp. today released software updates to plug at least 570 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, almost triple the number of vulnerabilities the software giant fixed in its record-smashing Patch Tuesday release last month. Microsoft attributed the burgeoning patch counts to vulnerability discoveries aided by artificial intelligence.

articles.headline: Lessons Learned from CISA’s Recent GitHub Leak
articles.blurb: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued a postmortem on a data leak in which a contractor published dozens of internal CISA credentials -- including AWS Govcloud keys -- in a public GitHub repository for almost six months before being notified by KrebsOnSecurity. Experts say the gaps identified in the agency's initial response provide important lessons that all security teams should absorb.

articles.headline: Felons, Fraudsters Flog Offensive Cybersecurity Startup
articles.blurb: A cybersecurity startup dangling millions of dollars to acquire zero-day security vulnerabilities in popular software is run by a pair of far-right conspiracy theorists and convicted felons whose most recent ventures included fake intelligence companies and a now-defunct AI-based lobbying platform they operated under assumed names.

articles.headline: FBI Seizes NetNut Proxy Platform, Popa Botnet
articles.blurb: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said today it worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, a sprawling residential proxy service operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies [NASDAQ: ALAR]. The action comes roughly two weeks after KrebsOnSecurity published findings from multiple security firms connecting NetNut to the Popa botnet, a collection of at least two million devices that have been compromised by malicious software with little or no consent from victims.

articles.headline: Scattered Spider Hackers Plead Guilty on Day 1 of Trial
articles.blurb: Two men pleaded guilty in the United Kingdom this week to criminal charges stemming from an August 2024 cyberattack that crippled Transport for London, the entity responsible for the public transport network in the Greater London area. The duo were key members of a prolific cybercrime group known as Scattered Spider, and their guilty pleas came on the first day of what was expected to be a six-week trial.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday.
